documents.title: IFRS 9 Corporates Reference Data Set documentation

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document is the reference data set (RDS) documentation of the IFRS 9 expected credit loss model for corporate and institutional clients (model identifier MDL-08, model name ECL-CORP, model version 2.0 in development) and follows the RDS template in Annex A of the Model Documentation Standard (MRM-STD-021). The RDS serves the development of the TTC-to-PIT conversion, the sector credit cycle indices and their satellite models, the conditional rating migration matrices, the LGD and CCF components and the staging module of version 2.0, which replaces the scalar approach of version 1.3 in production since 2021. Its scope is all loans and advances measured at amortised cost, loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts of the Bank to large corporates, mid-market corporates, banks and other financial institutions rated on the Bank master scale, which are within the scope of the IFRS 9 impairment requirements; debt securities are covered by a separate model. The model output is used to measure the 12-month and lifetime loss allowance for financial reporting under IFRS 9 and the IFRS 7 disclosures, with secondary use in the ICAAP and stress-test projections.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The frozen RDS (version RDS-ECLC-2025-v1.0) consists of quarterly snapshots from 31 March 2008 to 31 December 2025 (72 reference dates) at obligor and facility level, containing 498,600 obligor-quarters and 1.52 million facility-quarters, covering 11,930 unique obligors and 38,700 unique facilities. It contains 1,412 obligor default events after merging 63 re-defaults within 12 months of a cure, of which 1,130 workouts were closed by 31 December 2025 (463 cures and 667 liquidations or restructurings with loss). The observed annual obligor default rate ranges from 3.4% (2009) to 0.6% (2021), with a long-run average of 1.5% over 2008–2025 and 1.1% in 2025. At 31 December 2025 the portfolio comprised 6,720 obligors and 21,050 facilities with drawn exposure of EUR 37.9 billion; at 31 December 2026 it comprises 6,840 obligors and 21,400 facilities with EUR 38.6 billion drawn and EUR 14.2 billion undrawn commitments and guarantees.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in 2008, the first year for which the rating histories of the current IRB rating systems are available in the rating database, and covers the 2008–2009 financial crisis, the 2011–2013 euro area recession, the COVID-19 period and the 2022–2023 energy price and interest rate shock, i.e. a full economic cycle with good and bad years. The 18-year window exceeds the minimum of five years of FIN-STD-200 §11.2 and provides the variation in default rates across sectors needed to estimate the sector credit cycle indices. Historical conditions not relevant for the future are adjusted for: the 2008–2009 defaults of the shipping portfolio, which the Bank ran down after 2014, are retained for the estimation of the transport sector index but excluded from the calibration of the current grade PDs. The external long-run default and transition data used to stabilise the sector indices cover 1990–2025.

sections.heading: Development, out-of-time and calibration windows
sections.text: Within the RDS, the credit cycle indices and satellite models are estimated on 2008–2022, 2023–2025 is reserved as out-of-time sample, and the point-in-time calibration uses the default rates observed in 2023–2025. The LGD model is estimated on defaults of 2008–2022 with closed workouts and tested out of time on 2023–2025 closures, and the CCF on the 1,284 defaults with limit data available 12 months before default. The LGD segments (collateral type and seniority) and CCF segments (product type) are defined identically in the RDS and in the ECL engine and are linked at each reporting date to current collateral values and limits.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The PD target is the obligor default under CR-STD-110 within one year after the reference date; rating migration targets are the obligor grade one year after the reference date, with default as absorbing state. The outcome horizon of the lifetime term structure is the remaining contractual maturity of term facilities and, for revolving facilities that can be cancelled at short notice, the behavioural period of exposure described in section 4.5 of the MDD. The LGD target is the realised economic loss discounted at the effective interest rate, including directly attributable costs, and the CCF target is the drawdown of the undrawn limit between 12 months before default and default.

sections.heading: Past-due criterion and materiality threshold
sections.text: An obligor is in default when the materiality threshold of EUR 500 (absolute component) and 1% (relative component) has been exceeded for more than 90 consecutive days, or when the obligor is considered unlikely to pay under section 3.4. These are the single thresholds for exposures other than retail set by the ECB for significant institutions in Regulation (EU) 2018/1845, with the absolute component of EUR 500 and the relative component at 1%. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all past due amounts of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component equals that sum divided by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure, excluding equity exposures. The days-past-due counter starts on the first day on which both components are exceeded and is reset when either component is no longer exceeded. For facilities in US dollar and pound sterling (7% of exposure) past due amounts are converted to euro at the daily ECB reference rate, as the threshold is set in euro. The regulatory threshold has been applied from 1 November 2020; for 2016–2020 the RDS recomputes the default flag from the daily arrears ledger, and the variable MAT_REGIME identifies the threshold regime of each default event.

sections.heading: Days-past-due counting and technical past due
sections.text: Any amount of principal, interest or fees not paid on its due date is past due, and where the repayment schedule has been changed, days past due are counted on the modified schedule. Payment deferrals granted under the 2020 COVID-19 moratoria were not counted as past due, and each deferral was assessed by the relationship manager and Credit Risk Management for indications of unlikeliness to pay. Days past due are counted daily in the loan administration system, and the date of default in the RDS is the date on which the criterion was actually met, not the quarter-end. Technical past due is recognised only in the situations of paragraph 23 of EBA/GL/2016/07; each case is documented and corrected within 30 days, and the 214 cases in the RDS are not counted as defaults. Once the past due criterion is met, the obligor is defaulted without further judgement and all its exposures are flagged as defaulted.

sections.heading: Level of application, groups of connected clients
sections.text: Default is identified at obligor level for all exposure classes, and all credit obligations of a defaulted obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries are flagged as defaulted. The default of an obligor within a group of connected clients does not automatically lead to the default of other group entities; CR-STD-110 §6.2 requires a case-by-case UTP assessment of each connected obligor within 30 days, taking into account financial dependency and cross-default clauses. The group structure is available in the client database from 2014; for 2008–2013 contagion effects cannot be reconstructed (deficiency DD-03). The Default Register is the authoritative source and propagates the default status daily to all systems of the Bank and its foreign branches, so that the default is identified consistently across legal entities and locations. For the branches in Belgium and Germany there are no legal impediments to the exchange of client data within the Bank.

sections.heading: Probation, multiple defaults and historical approximation
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-default status only after at least three months without any default trigger and an assessment by Credit Risk Management that the improvement in credit quality is factual and permanent. After a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least 12 months from the latest of the restructuring, the end of the grace period and the default, and return requires a material payment, regular payments under the new schedule, no past due amount and no doubt about full repayment. The probation start date and status are recorded for every default event, and re-defaults within 12 months after cure are merged with the original default (63 merges). For 2008–2015 the default flag is approximated from the watchlist category 'Restricted', the arrears history above 90 days and the restructuring and impairment flags; on the 2016 overlap the approximation identifies 5.8% fewer defaults than the full definition, which is recorded as deficiency DD-01. Probation periods cannot be reconstructed for 2008–2015, for which cure is approximated by removal from the 'Restricted' category for two consecutive quarters.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: The automatic UTP triggers of CR-STD-110 §6.1 apply: non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments including Stage 3 allowances, a sale at a credit-related economic loss above 5%, a distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%, bankruptcy or similar protection and the forced sale of collateral or calling of a guarantee. Stage 1 and Stage 2 allowances are not specific credit risk adjustments and do not trigger default, and all Stage 3 exposures are defaulted without the exceptions of paragraph 39 of EBA/GL/2016/07. The indicators of CR-STD-110 §6.2 (fraud, significant decline in cash flow, breach of material covenants, multiple forbearance, default of a connected obligor, default at another institution and loss of a major customer) lead to a case-by-case assessment by Credit Risk Management within 30 days, whose outcome and rationale are recorded in the credit workflow system. UTP identification uses external information: rating agency actions, press and analyst reports screened by the early-warning system, the Central Insolvency Register and sector information from Credit Risk Management. Each trigger and indicator is mapped to source-system fields, and the triggers are applied identically in the RDS construction and in production.

sections.heading: Forbearance, sales and restructuring
sections.text: The diminished financial obligation of each forbearance measure is calculated as (NPV0 − NPV1)/NPV0 with both net present values discounted at the original effective interest rate, and measures above 1% lead to default. Measures below the threshold are assessed for other UTP indications such as a large bullet, back-loaded schedules, long grace periods and repeated forbearance. All forborne non-performing exposures are defaulted, which Credit Risk Management verifies monthly, and forborne performing exposures are reviewed quarterly. The Bank sold 38 non-performing corporate exposures in 2014–2019; for each sale the reasons were analysed and the credit-related loss L = (E − P)/E calculated, and the 31 sales with a loss above 5% were treated as defaults at the date of sale where no earlier default had been identified.

sections.heading: Source systems and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is built from the rating database RDB (domain Ratings, Data Owner Head of Credit Risk Management), the corporate loan administration system CLA (domain Corporate Loans, Head of Corporate Lending Operations), the collateral management system CMS (domain Collateral), the Default Register (domain Credit Risk Status), the finance subledger (domain Finance) and the scenario store ESS (domain Macroeconomic Scenarios), each with one Data Owner in the Group Data Catalogue. The model owner agreed the data quality expectations for the 41 critical data elements with the Data Owners in data quality agreements DQA-CORP-2026-01 to -06. Lineage from source field to RDS variable is documented for every variable, including discarded variables such as the individual financial statement items used to derive the leverage ratio, in Annex A and in the Group Data Catalogue lineage tool. sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document is the reference data set (RDS) documentation of the IFRS 9 expected credit loss model for corporate and institutional clients (model identifier MDL-08, model name ECL-CORP, model version 2.0 in development) and follows the RDS template in Annex A of the Model Documentation Standard (MRM-STD-021). The RDS serves the development of the TTC-to-PIT conversion, the sector credit cycle indices and their satellite models, the conditional rating migration matrices, the LGD and CCF components and the staging module of version 2.0, which replaces the scalar approach of version 1.3 in production since 2021. Its scope is all loans and advances measured at amortised cost, loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts of the Bank to large corporates, mid-market corporates, banks and other financial institutions rated on the Bank master scale, which are within the scope of the IFRS 9 impairment requirements; debt securities are covered by a separate model. The model output is used to measure the 12-month and lifetime loss allowance for financial reporting under IFRS 9 and the IFRS 7 disclosures, with secondary use in the ICAAP and stress-test projections.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in 2008, the first year for which the rating histories of the current IRB rating systems are available in the rating database, and covers the 2008–2009 financial crisis, the 2011–2013 euro area recession, the COVID-19 period and the 2022–2023 energy price and interest rate shock, i.e. a full economic cycle with good and bad years. The 18-year window exceeds the minimum of five years of FIN-STD-200 §11.2 and provides the variation in default rates across sectors needed to estimate the sector credit cycle indices. Historical conditions not relevant for the future are adjusted for: the 2008–2009 defaults of the shipping portfolio, which the Bank ran down after 2014, are retained for the estimation of the transport sector index but excluded from the calibration of the current grade PDs. The external long-run default and transition data used to stabilise the sector indices cover 1990–2025.

sections.heading: Past-due criterion and materiality threshold
sections.text: An obligor is in default when the materiality threshold of EUR 500 (absolute component) and 1% (relative component) has been exceeded for more than 90 consecutive days, or when the obligor is considered unlikely to pay under section 3.4. These are the single thresholds for exposures other than retail set by the ECB for significant institutions in Regulation (EU) 2018/1845, with the absolute component of EUR 500 and the relative component at 1%. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all past due amounts of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component equals that sum divided by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure, excluding equity exposures. The days-past-due counter starts on the first day on which both components are exceeded and is reset when either component is no longer exceeded. For facilities in US dollar and pound sterling (7% of exposure) past due amounts are converted to euro at the daily ECB reference rate, as the threshold is set in euro. The regulatory threshold has been applied from 1 November 2020; for 2016–2020 the RDS recomputes the default flag from the daily arrears ledger, and the variable MAT_REGIME identifies the threshold regime of each default event.

sections.heading: Days-past-due counting and technical past due
sections.text: Any amount of principal, interest or fees not paid on its due date is past due, and where the repayment schedule has been changed, days past due are counted on the modified schedule. Payment deferrals granted under the 2020 COVID-19 moratoria were not counted as past due, and each deferral was assessed by the relationship manager and Credit Risk Management for indications of unlikeliness to pay. Days past due are counted daily in the loan administration system, and the date of default in the RDS is the date on which the criterion was actually met, not the quarter-end. Technical past due is recognised only in the situations of paragraph 23 of EBA/GL/2016/07; each case is documented and corrected within 30 days, and the 214 cases in the RDS are not counted as defaults. Once the past due criterion is met, the obligor is defaulted without further judgement and all its exposures are flagged as defaulted.

sections.heading: Level of application, groups of connected clients
sections.text: Default is identified at obligor level for all exposure classes, and all credit obligations of a defaulted obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries are flagged as defaulted. The default of an obligor within a group of connected clients does not automatically lead to the default of other group entities; CR-STD-110 §6.2 requires a case-by-case UTP assessment of each connected obligor within 30 days, taking into account financial dependency and cross-default clauses. The group structure is available in the client database from 2014; for 2008–2013 contagion effects cannot be reconstructed (deficiency DD-03). The Default Register is the authoritative source and propagates the default status daily to all systems of the Bank and its foreign branches, so that the default is identified consistently across legal entities and locations. For the branches in Belgium and Germany there are no legal impediments to the exchange of client data within the Bank.

sections.heading: Probation, multiple defaults and historical approximation
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-default status only after at least three months without any default trigger and an assessment by Credit Risk Management that the improvement in credit quality is factual and permanent. After a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least 12 months from the latest of the restructuring, the end of the grace period and the default, and return requires a material payment, regular payments under the new schedule, no past due amount and no doubt about full repayment. The probation start date and status are recorded for every default event, and re-defaults within 12 months after cure are merged with the original default (63 merges). For 2008–2015 the default flag is approximated from the watchlist category 'Restricted', the arrears history above 90 days and the restructuring and impairment flags; on the 2016 overlap the approximation identifies 5.8% fewer defaults than the full definition, which is recorded as deficiency DD-01. Probation periods cannot be reconstructed for 2008–2015, for which cure is approximated by removal from the 'Restricted' category for two consecutive quarters. The RDS default flag is reconciled with the production flag for 2016–2025: 99.1% of default events agree on obligor and quarter, and the differences are explained by retroactive corrections.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: The automatic UTP triggers of CR-STD-110 §6.1 apply: non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments including Stage 3 allowances, a sale at a credit-related economic loss above 5%, a distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%, bankruptcy or similar protection and the forced sale of collateral or calling of a guarantee. Stage 1 and Stage 2 allowances are not specific credit risk adjustments and do not trigger default, and all Stage 3 exposures are defaulted without the exceptions of paragraph 39 of EBA/GL/2016/07. The indicators of CR-STD-110 §6.2 (fraud, significant decline in cash flow, breach of material covenants, multiple forbearance, default of a connected obligor, default at another institution and loss of a major customer) lead to a case-by-case assessment by Credit Risk Management within 30 days, whose outcome and rationale are recorded in the credit workflow system. UTP identification uses external information: rating agency actions, press and analyst reports screened by the early-warning system, the Central Insolvency Register and sector information from Credit Risk Management. Each trigger and indicator is mapped to source-system fields, and the triggers are applied identically in the RDS construction and in production.

sections.heading: Forbearance, sales and restructuring
sections.text: The diminished financial obligation of each forbearance measure is calculated as (NPV0 − NPV1)/NPV0 with both net present values discounted at the original effective interest rate, and measures above 1% lead to default. Measures below the threshold are assessed for other UTP indications such as a large bullet, back-loaded schedules, long grace periods and repeated forbearance. All forborne non-performing exposures are defaulted, which Credit Risk Management verifies monthly, and forborne performing exposures are reviewed quarterly. The Bank sold 38 non-performing corporate exposures in 2014–2019; for each sale the reasons were analysed and the credit-related loss L = (E − P)/E calculated, and the 31 sales with a loss above 5% were treated as defaults at the date of sale where no earlier default had been identified.

sections.heading: Source systems and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is built from the rating database RDB (domain Ratings, Data Owner Head of Credit Risk Management), the corporate loan administration system CLA (domain Corporate Loans, Head of Corporate Lending Operations), the collateral management system CMS (domain Collateral), the Default Register (domain Credit Risk Status), the finance subledger (domain Finance) and the scenario store ESS (domain Macroeconomic Scenarios), each with one Data Owner in the Group Data Catalogue. The model owner agreed the data quality expectations for the 41 critical data elements with the Data Owners in data quality agreements DQA-CORP-2026-01 to -06. Lineage from source field to RDS variable is documented for every variable, including discarded variables such as the individual financial statement items used to derive the leverage ratio, in Annex A and in the Group Data Catalogue lineage tool. For each variable the lineage identifies the source system and fields, the intermediate Risk Data Hub stores, each transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the build script, and the extraction frequency and timing. Changes to data elements are approved by the Data Owner and notified in advance to the model owner, and the lineage is updated before the changed data are used, as for the migration of the rating database to RDB 5 in May 2026.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are documented per variable in Annex C, distinguishing missing at random (for example the external rating, absent for 71% of obligors), structurally missing (collateral value for unsecured facilities) and missing due to data deficiencies (the limit history before 2011, deficiency DD-02). Missing limits before 2011 are not imputed; the CCF is estimated on 2011–2025 defaults only, which is documented as a data treatment and its effect assessed as immaterial. Outliers are identified with documented rules (CCF outside [0, 1.5] and realised LGD outside [−0.1, 1.2]) applied identically in development and production, and CCFs are capped at 1 and LGDs floored at 0 for estimation, which changes the estimated average CCF by −0.8 percentage points. Target values are not imputed: 11 defaults with missing default dates and 23 workouts with inconsistent recovery flows were corrected at source after investigation.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: ECL-CORP measures the loss allowance for expected credit losses on loans and advances at amortised cost, loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts to corporate and institutional clients rated on the Bank master scale. For loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts, the date on which the Bank becomes party to the irrevocable commitment is the date of initial recognition for impairment and the reference point of the SICR assessment. At 31 December 2026 the portfolio comprises 6,840 obligors (1,180 large corporates, 4,920 mid-market corporates and 740 banks and other financial institutions) and 21,400 facilities with EUR 38.6 billion drawn and EUR 14.2 billion undrawn commitments and guarantees; the loss allowance under version 1.3 is EUR 312 million, of which EUR 203 million Stage 3 (EUR 188 million individually assessed). Main users are Finance Reporting, Credit Risk Management and Enterprise Stress Testing; the model is used for IFRS 9 financial reporting and IFRS 7 disclosures and not for credit decisions. The expected credit loss and cost-of-risk metrics of the corporate portfolio in the credit risk appetite statement will be measured with this registered model once approved under MRM-POL-001.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: ECL is measured with a PD/LGD/EAD approach at facility level in quarterly time steps and probability-weighted over three scenarios, which is appropriate for a low-default rated portfolio in which the Bank's rating grades and sector conditions are the main drivers of credit risk; a loss-rate method was rejected because it cannot reflect grade migration. The components are: (1) TTC grade PDs from the IRB rating systems without prudential adjustments; (2) sector credit cycle indices Z and their satellite models; (3) Z-conditional rating migration matrices for the lifetime PD term structure; (4) the LGD model by collateral type; (5) the EAD and CCF model including the behavioural life of revolving facilities; (6) the staging module; and (7) the ECL aggregation in the ECL engine. For Stage 1 the 12-month ECL is the lifetime cash shortfall of defaults occurring in the next 12 months weighted by their probability, not the shortfall expected over the next 12 months. Stage 3 exposures of obligors with total exposure of EUR 1 million or more are measured individually by the workout function with probability-weighted discounted cash flows and are outside the modelled components.

sections.heading: Stage allocation
sections.text: At each reporting date facilities are allocated to Stage 3 if the obligor is in default, to Stage 2 if a Stage 2 criterion of section 4.2 is met, and otherwise to Stage 1; Stage 1 carries 12-month ECL and Stages 2 and 3 lifetime ECL. A facility returns to Stage 1 as soon as no Stage 2 criterion is met, without additional probation other than the forborne-performing period, and leaves Stage 3 only after the probation period of CR-STD-110. As the quantitative criterion uses the probability-weighted forward-looking lifetime PD, complemented by backstops and collective transfers, lifetime ECL is recognised for all facilities with a significant increase in credit risk, assessed individually or collectively. sections.heading: Methodological alternatives and selection
sections.text: Three methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation): (A) the scalar approach of version 1.3, which multiplies the IRB PD by a portfolio PIT/TTC scalar and extrapolates with a constant hazard; (B) TTC-to-PIT conversion by sector with a single-factor Z-shift of the rating migration matrices; and (C) sector-level survival models on obligor data. Approach B was selected: it reproduces the 2023–2025 sector default rates with a mean absolute error of 0.21 percentage points against 0.48 for approach A, produces grade migration and hence Stage 2 transfers consistent with the rating process, and remains interpretable; approach C was rejected because 1,412 defaults over eight sectors do not support stable survival models. sections.heading: SICR – quantitative criterion and thresholds
sections.text: The SICR test compares the annualised remaining-lifetime PD at the reporting date with the annualised lifetime PD expected at initial recognition for the same remaining term, both probability-weighted, so that the change in the risk of default over the expected life is assessed on a consistent remaining-life basis. A significant increase is identified when the ratio of current to origination annualised lifetime PD exceeds 2.0 and the absolute increase exceeds 0.40 percentage points; the relative threshold makes a given increase more significant for obligors originated with low default risk. The thresholds were calibrated on 2016–2025 on the trade-off between capture rate (78% of defaults in Stage 2 at least six months before default) and stage volatility (7.9%), against 84%/14.2% for 1.5/0.25 and 66%/4.8% for 2.5/0.60, and will be re-assessed annually. The test is based on the risk of default before collateral and guarantees, not on the change in expected credit losses. For facilities originated before 2018 the origination lifetime PD is derived from the origination grade and the Z of the origination quarter; stage allocation agrees for 96.9% of 2018–2019 originations where both are available.

sections.heading: SICR – backstops, qualitative indicators and collective assessment
sections.text: A performing facility is in Stage 2 when the obligor is more than 30 days past due on a material amount, when forbearance has been granted (for the two-year probation period) or when the obligor is on the watchlist in categories 'Watch' or 'Restricted'. The 30-days-past-due presumption is a backstop only: 94% of facilities reaching 30 days past due in 2025 were already in Stage 2, and the presumption is not rebutted. The assessment is multifactor: rating downgrades reflect financial performance and covenant information, the watchlist reflects early-warning signals, and collective transfers reflect sector deterioration identified by Credit Risk Management, so that the indicators of IFRS 9 B5.5.17 relevant to corporates are considered. Obligors triggering the early-warning indicators (payment delays, covenant breaches, rating agency downgrades and negative news) are assessed within 30 days and placed on the watchlist where deterioration is confirmed. Where sector information indicates increased credit risk not yet reflected in individual ratings, SICR is assessed collectively for the affected sub-group, as for the real estate developers transferred to Stage 2 in 2026, with the population, evidence and review date recorded. The criteria transfer exposures well before default; SICR recognition is not aligned with the point of default.

sections.heading: Sector credit cycle indices and satellite models
sections.text: For each sector group a credit cycle index Z is estimated from the internal and external annual default and migration rates of 2008–2022 with the single-factor model PD_PIT = Φ((Φ⁻¹(PD_TTC) − √ρ Z)/√(1 − ρ)), with sector asset correlations ρ between 0.08 (healthcare) and 0.19 (real estate). Each Z is linked by a satellite regression to macroeconomic variables selected from 16 candidates for economic intuition, expected sign, significance and out-of-time performance: euro area GDP growth and sector gross value added growth for all sectors, the 10-year swap rate and house prices for real estate, and energy prices for industry and utilities; rejected candidates (unemployment, equity index, credit spreads) are documented with the reasons. For transport and logistics, the gross value added coefficient is not significant (p = 0.14) but is retained on economic grounds as expert judgement EJ-MDD-03. Out of time (2023–2025) the satellite models predict the annual sector default rates with a mean absolute error of 0.21 percentage points.

sections.heading: Lifetime PD term structure
sections.text: Lifetime PD term structures per grade and sector are obtained by multiplying one-year TTC migration matrices (13 states including default, estimated on 2008–2022 cohorts) shifted by the scenario-specific Z of each year, which gives point-in-time PD term structures over the expected life of each facility. Over the reasonable and supportable forecast period of three years (36 months) the scenario Z paths are used; over the following 24 months Z reverts linearly to zero, after which the unshifted TTC matrix applies, so that the ECL of facilities with lives beyond the forecast horizon is estimated with a documented reversion. Cumulative PDs are monotonically non-decreasing and marginal PDs non-negative by construction of the Markov chain, which the engine verifies at each run. Prepayment of term loans is reflected in the EAD profile through a constant annual prepayment rate of 6% per client type estimated on 2014–2025.

sections.heading: LGD
sections.text: LGD is estimated by collateral type (unsecured, commercial real estate, other physical collateral, financial collateral and guarantees) as a cure-weighted workout LGD with collateral recoveries based on current collateral values and scenario-specific property price paths, including proceeds from collateral and guarantees that are part of the contractual terms. The LGD is a best estimate without downturn adjustment, margin of conservatism or regulatory floors, and recoveries and costs are discounted at the effective interest rate. Facilities are written off when there is no reasonable expectation of recovery, and post-write-off recoveries are included in realised LGD consistently with this policy. The average LGD of performing facilities is 27.4% in the baseline, 24.9% in the upside and 31.8% in the downside scenario, based on 1,130 closed workouts with a cure rate of 41%.

sections.heading: EAD and behavioural life
sections.text: EAD follows the contractual schedule for term loans with prepayments and accrued interest, and CCFs estimated on the Bank's drawdown experience for undrawn limits (0.52 for revolving credit facilities and overdrafts, 0.30 for financial guarantees), without regulatory floors. For term facilities the ECL horizon is the remaining contractual maturity and never exceeds the maximum contractual period. For revolving credit facilities and overdrafts that can be cancelled at short notice, the measurement period is the behavioural period of exposure of 36 months, estimated from the time between origination or last credit review and default or closure in 2011–2025, and not the contractual notice period, reflecting that the annual credit review does not in practice limit exposure earlier.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: ECL-CORP measures the loss allowance for expected credit losses on loans and advances at amortised cost, loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts to corporate and institutional clients rated on the Bank master scale. For loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts, the date on which the Bank becomes party to the irrevocable commitment is the date of initial recognition for impairment and the reference point of the SICR assessment. At 31 December 2026 the portfolio comprises 6,840 obligors (1,180 large corporates, 4,920 mid-market corporates and 740 banks and other financial institutions) and 21,400 facilities with EUR 38.6 billion drawn and EUR 14.2 billion undrawn commitments and guarantees; the loss allowance under version 1.3 is EUR 312 million, of which EUR 203 million Stage 3 (EUR 188 million individually assessed). Main users are Finance Reporting, Credit Risk Management and Enterprise Stress Testing; the model is used for IFRS 9 financial reporting and IFRS 7 disclosures and not for credit decisions. The expected credit loss and cost-of-risk metrics of the corporate portfolio in the credit risk appetite statement will be measured with this registered model once approved under MRM-POL-001.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: ECL is measured with a PD/LGD/EAD approach at facility level in quarterly time steps and probability-weighted over three scenarios, which is appropriate for a low-default rated portfolio in which the Bank's rating grades and sector conditions are the main drivers of credit risk; a loss-rate method was rejected because it cannot reflect grade migration. The components are: (1) TTC grade PDs from the IRB rating systems without prudential adjustments; (2) sector credit cycle indices Z and their satellite models; (3) Z-conditional rating migration matrices for the lifetime PD term structure; (4) the LGD model by collateral type; (5) the EAD and CCF model including the behavioural life of revolving facilities; (6) the staging module; and (7) the ECL aggregation in the ECL engine. For Stage 1 the 12-month ECL is the lifetime cash shortfall of defaults occurring in the next 12 months weighted by their probability, not the shortfall expected over the next 12 months. Stage 3 exposures of obligors with total exposure of EUR 1 million or more are measured individually by the workout function with probability-weighted discounted cash flows and are outside the modelled components.

sections.heading: Segmentation and dependencies
sections.text: Obligors are grouped by client type and eight sector groups (real estate and construction; industry; trade; transport and logistics; energy and utilities; technology, media and telecoms; healthcare and services; financial institutions), which share credit cycle sensitivity, and by grade, so that the groups are granular enough to detect changes in credit risk while staging remains at facility level. The model depends on the IRB corporate rating systems (large corporate, mid-corporate and financial institutions), the scenario models of Enterprise Stress Testing and the Default Register, and uses the same rating, default and collateral data as credit risk management and the capital calculation. Rating inputs follow CR-POL-001: non-retail ratings are reviewed at least annually and semi-annually for watchlist obligors, and ratings older than 12 months are expired; the ECL engine applies a one-notch downgrade to expired ratings, which affected 1.8% of obligors at 31 December 2026. Ratings are assigned or approved by Credit Risk Management independently of the commercial function, and upward rating overrides of more than two notches require Group Credit Committee approval, so that the grade inputs used by the model are independently assigned.

sections.heading: Stage allocation
sections.text: At each reporting date facilities are allocated to Stage 3 if the obligor is in default, to Stage 2 if a Stage 2 criterion of section 4.2 is met, and otherwise to Stage 1; Stage 1 carries 12-month ECL and Stages 2 and 3 lifetime ECL. A facility returns to Stage 1 as soon as no Stage 2 criterion is met, without additional probation other than the forborne-performing period, and leaves Stage 3 only after the probation period of CR-STD-110. As the quantitative criterion uses the probability-weighted forward-looking lifetime PD, complemented by backstops and collective transfers, lifetime ECL is recognised for all facilities with a significant increase in credit risk, assessed individually or collectively. Under version 2.0 at 31 December 2026, Stage 1 comprises EUR 33.3 billion (86.2% of drawn exposure), Stage 2 EUR 4.5 billion (11.7%) and Stage 3 EUR 0.8 billion (2.1%), against 87.8%, 10.1% and 2.1% under version 1.3.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives and selection
sections.text: Three methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation): (A) the scalar approach of version 1.3, which multiplies the IRB PD by a portfolio PIT/TTC scalar and extrapolates with a constant hazard; (B) TTC-to-PIT conversion by sector with a single-factor Z-shift of the rating migration matrices; and (C) sector-level survival models on obligor data. Approach B was selected: it reproduces the 2023–2025 sector default rates with a mean absolute error of 0.21 percentage points against 0.48 for approach A, produces grade migration and hence Stage 2 transfers consistent with the rating process, and remains interpretable; approach C was rejected because 1,412 defaults over eight sectors do not support stable survival models. The change from A to B increases the modelled Stage 1 and 2 ECL at 31 December 2026 from EUR 109 million to EUR 121 million, mainly through higher Stage 2 transfers in real estate and transport.

sections.heading: SICR – quantitative criterion and thresholds
sections.text: The SICR test compares the annualised remaining-lifetime PD at the reporting date with the annualised lifetime PD expected at initial recognition for the same remaining term, both probability-weighted, so that the change in the risk of default over the expected life is assessed on a consistent remaining-life basis. A significant increase is identified when the ratio of current to origination annualised lifetime PD exceeds 2.0 and the absolute increase exceeds 0.40 percentage points; the relative threshold makes a given increase more significant for obligors originated with low default risk. The thresholds were calibrated on 2016–2025 on the trade-off between capture rate (78% of defaults in Stage 2 at least six months before default) and stage volatility (7.9%), against 84%/14.2% for 1.5/0.25 and 66%/4.8% for 2.5/0.60, and will be re-assessed annually. The test is based on the risk of default before collateral and guarantees, not on the change in expected credit losses. For facilities originated before 2018 the origination lifetime PD is derived from the origination grade and the Z of the origination quarter; stage allocation agrees for 96.9% of 2018–2019 originations where both are available.

sections.heading: SICR – backstops, qualitative indicators and collective assessment
sections.text: A performing facility is in Stage 2 when the obligor is more than 30 days past due on a material amount, when forbearance has been granted (for the two-year probation period) or when the obligor is on the watchlist in categories 'Watch' or 'Restricted'. The 30-days-past-due presumption is a backstop only: 94% of facilities reaching 30 days past due in 2025 were already in Stage 2, and the presumption is not rebutted. The assessment is multifactor: rating downgrades reflect financial performance and covenant information, the watchlist reflects early-warning signals, and collective transfers reflect sector deterioration identified by Credit Risk Management, so that the indicators of IFRS 9 B5.5.17 relevant to corporates are considered. Obligors triggering the early-warning indicators (payment delays, covenant breaches, rating agency downgrades and negative news) are assessed within 30 days and placed on the watchlist where deterioration is confirmed. Where sector information indicates increased credit risk not yet reflected in individual ratings, SICR is assessed collectively for the affected sub-group, as for the real estate developers transferred to Stage 2 in 2026, with the population, evidence and review date recorded. The criteria transfer exposures well before default; SICR recognition is not aligned with the point of default.

sections.heading: Low credit risk and modified assets
sections.text: The low credit risk exemption is not applied to loans and advances, in accordance with FIN-STD-200 §5.7, so every facility is subject to the SICR test. Investment-grade external ratings of borrowers do not exempt facilities from the SICR test, which is based on the Bank's internal rating. For modifications that do not result in derecognition, SICR compares the lifetime PD under the modified terms with the origination PD under the original terms. Modified facilities are not considered lower risk automatically: forborne facilities remain in Stage 2 for the probation period, and return requires timely performance under the modified terms.

sections.heading: TTC PD and prudential adjustments
sections.text: The TTC PD per grade is derived from the IRB rating systems with each IFRS 9 adjustment documented: the margin of conservatism of the IRB calibration (on average +11% relative) is removed by using the grade PDs before MoC, the regulatory PD floor of 0.05% is not applied, and no downturn component exists in the IRB PD. Removing the margin of conservatism reduces the modelled ECL at 31 December 2026 by EUR 9.4 million. The TTC grade PDs range from 0.03% (MS01) to 22% (MS12). Differences between IFRS 9 and IRB design choices (point-in-time versus long-run PD, lifetime horizon, effective interest rate discounting and best-estimate LGD instead of the supervisory LGD) are reconciled in section 4.8, with rationale approved by the Group Impairment Committee.

sections.heading: Sector credit cycle indices and satellite models
sections.text: For each sector group a credit cycle index Z is estimated from the internal and external annual default and migration rates of 2008–2022 with the single-factor model PD_PIT = Φ((Φ⁻¹(PD_TTC) − √ρ Z)/√(1 − ρ)), with sector asset correlations ρ between 0.08 (healthcare) and 0.19 (real estate). Each Z is linked by a satellite regression to macroeconomic variables selected from 16 candidates for economic intuition, expected sign, significance and out-of-time performance: euro area GDP growth and sector gross value added growth for all sectors, the 10-year swap rate and house prices for real estate, and energy prices for industry and utilities; rejected candidates (unemployment, equity index, credit spreads) are documented with the reasons. For transport and logistics, the gross value added coefficient is not significant (p = 0.14) but is retained on economic grounds as expert judgement EJ-MDD-03. Out of time (2023–2025) the satellite models predict the annual sector default rates with a mean absolute error of 0.21 percentage points.

sections.heading: Lifetime PD term structure
sections.text: Lifetime PD term structures per grade and sector are obtained by multiplying one-year TTC migration matrices (13 states including default, estimated on 2008–2022 cohorts) shifted by the scenario-specific Z of each year, which gives point-in-time PD term structures over the expected life of each facility. Over the reasonable and supportable forecast period of three years (36 months) the scenario Z paths are used; over the following 24 months Z reverts linearly to zero, after which the unshifted TTC matrix applies, so that the ECL of facilities with lives beyond the forecast horizon is estimated with a documented reversion. Cumulative PDs are monotonically non-decreasing and marginal PDs non-negative by construction of the Markov chain, which the engine verifies at each run. Prepayment of term loans is reflected in the EAD profile through a constant annual prepayment rate of 6% per client type estimated on 2014–2025.

sections.heading: Point-in-time calibration
sections.text: The one-year PIT PDs are calibrated to the default rates observed in 2023–2025 per sector group adjusted to current conditions through the current Z; the long-run average default rate is not used as calibration target. After calibration the predicted 2025 default rate is 1.14% against 1.10% observed at portfolio level. Per sector the largest difference is in real estate and construction (predicted 1.9%, observed 2.3%), which is within the confidence interval of the calibration test (section 7.1).

sections.heading: LGD
sections.text: LGD is estimated by collateral type (unsecured, commercial real estate, other physical collateral, financial collateral and guarantees) as a cure-weighted workout LGD with collateral recoveries based on current collateral values and scenario-specific property price paths, including proceeds from collateral and guarantees that are part of the contractual terms. The LGD is a best estimate without downturn adjustment, margin of conservatism or regulatory floors, and recoveries and costs are discounted at the effective interest rate. Facilities are written off when there is no reasonable expectation of recovery, and post-write-off recoveries are included in realised LGD consistently with this policy. The average LGD of performing facilities is 27.4% in the baseline, 24.9% in the upside and 31.8% in the downside scenario, based on 1,130 closed workouts with a cure rate of 41%.

sections.heading: EAD and behavioural life
sections.text: EAD follows the contractual schedule for term loans with prepayments and accrued interest, and CCFs estimated on the Bank's drawdown experience for undrawn limits (0.52 for revolving credit facilities and overdrafts, 0.30 for financial guarantees), without regulatory floors. For term facilities the ECL horizon is the remaining contractual maturity and never exceeds the maximum contractual period. For revolving credit facilities and overdrafts that can be cancelled at short notice, the measurement period is the behavioural period of exposure of 36 months, estimated from the time between origination or last credit review and default or closure in 2011–2025, and not the contractual notice period, reflecting that the annual credit review does not in practice limit exposure earlier.

The average one-year PD of performing obligors is 0.92% under the baseline, 0.78% under the upside and 1.46% under the downside, which shows how PD, and through collateral prices LGD, change with the scenarios. Every facility carries a positive PD in all scenarios, so the estimate reflects both the possibility of loss and of no loss. documents.title: Data quality assessment report – IFRS 9 Corporates RDS 2025

sections.heading: Scope and approach
sections.text: This report documents the data quality assessment of the frozen RDS RDS-ECLC-2025-v1.0 of model MDL-08, performed before the development of version 2.0 in accordance with MRM-STD-022 §5.1. The assessment was performed by IFRS 9 Modelling (Ruben Vermeulen) with the Data Stewards of the six data domains between 3 and 17 February 2027 and covers 498,600 obligor-quarters, 1.52 million facility-quarters and 1,412 default events over 2008–2025. Results per rule, variable and dimension are reported in the annex; the sections below summarise them.

evidence.quote: This report documents the data quality assessment of the frozen RDS RDS-ECLC-2025-v1.0 of model MDL-08, performed before the development of version 2.0 in accordance with MRM-STD-022 §5.1.

sections.heading: Critical data elements, rules and thresholds
sections.text: The 41 critical data elements have 187 rules, at least one per applicable mandatory dimension, defined jointly with the Data Stewards and documented in the RDS documentation; recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool. Each rule has amber and red thresholds at least as strict as the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3, and the target constituents (default flag, default date, EAD, recoveries, costs and limits) have stricter thresholds of 99.5% and 99% for completeness. For the timeliness of financial statements the rule uses an amber threshold of 15 months and a red threshold of 18 months, which is less strict than the default refresh-plus-one-month rule because statements are published up to six months after year-end; the deviation was justified and approved by the model owner and by Model Risk Management on 10 February 2027.

sections.heading: Change summary
sections.text: This change memorandum describes the redevelopment of the IFRS 9 corporate ECL model from version 1.3 to version 2.0 (change CHG-2026-0231), recorded in the change log of the model inventory on 5 October 2026, before any implementation. It describes the change and its rationale, the affected components and documents, the internal classification with analysis, the quantitative impact, the required validation and the implementation plan. The memo was prepared by Ruben Vermeulen and approved by Maarten Hoekstra on 21 May 2027 after MRM's confirmation of the classification.

sections.heading: Rationale
sections.text: The annual validation 2026 of version 1.3 (report VAL-2026-051, opinion 'fit for purpose with conditions' of 29 October 2026) found that the portfolio-wide PIT/TTC scalar did not capture sector-specific cycles and that the constant-hazard lifetime extension underestimated Stage 2 lifetime PDs; condition MRC-C-2026-034 requires the redevelopment to be approved by 31 December 2027. The real estate overlay of EUR 24 million had been in place since Q1 2026 because of this limitation. The redevelopment, the removal of the real estate overlay and the new LGD model by collateral type, which address the same validation findings, are recorded and assessed together as a single change.

evidence.quote: The redevelopment, the removal of the real estate overlay and the new LGD model by collateral type, which address the same validation findings, are recorded and assessed together as a single change.

sections.heading: Affected components and documents
sections.text: Affected components: PIT PD methodology, lifetime PD term structure, SICR thresholds, LGD model, CCF and behavioural life of revolving facilities, and the ECL engine parameter loader; unchanged: the definition of default, the rating systems as inputs, the scenarios and the individual Stage 3 assessment. Affected documents: the new RDS documentation EVD-08-RDS, the MDD EVD-08-MDD version 1.0, the implementation specification EVD-08-IS, the monitoring plan (MDD chapter 10), the ECL operating procedure and the overlay register. New input sources: the licensed external rating agency default and transition study and sector gross value added series.

sections.heading: Classification
sections.text: The change is classified as internally material because it changes the methodology and risk drivers and introduces a new material input source, irrespective of its output impact. The impact at 31 December 2026 is +11% on the modelled Stage 1 and 2 ECL (EUR 109 million to EUR 121 million) and +3.8% on the total loss allowance, with 6.2% of exposure changing stage, which exceeds the 5% output threshold of MRM-STD-050 §5.2(e). No regulatory class applies because the IFRS 9 model does not require supervisory permission; the change has not been split, and the cumulative impact of the changes since the last full validation of version 1.0 has been included. MRM confirmed the classification on 3 November 2026.

sections.heading: Transformations and calculation steps
sections.text: The specification defines every transformation, missing-value and outlier treatment (including the one-notch downgrade for expired ratings, the CCF cap and the LGD floor), formula, coefficient, lookup table, sector mapping and grade scale, with precision (double) and rounding conventions (ECL rounded to cents at output only). The calculation steps are: Z per sector and scenario, conditional migration matrices per year, marginal and cumulative PD per grade and sector, EAD profile per facility, LGD per collateral type and scenario, discounting at the effective interest rate and probability weighting. Stage allocation follows section 2.3 and 4.2 of the MDD, with the thresholds held in the parameter table.

sections.text: Any difference between production code, this specification and the MDD will be treated as a defect or submitted as a model change under MRM-STD-050. deficiencies.rationale: MDD section 4.3.1 documents and quantifies the removal of the IRB margin of conservatism (−EUR 9.4 million), but the effect of not applying the 0.05% PD floor is only stated, not quantified, although it affects the MS01–MS02 grades of the financial institutions segment.

mitigation.text: Quantify the ECL effect of removing the regulatory PD floor per client type and add it to MDD section 4.3.1.

deficiencies.rationale: The transport sector satellite model retains gross value added with p = 0.14 (EJ-MDD-03); FIN-STD-200 §9.5 requires statistically significant variables, and the retention is justified only by economic intuition.

mitigation.text: Test alternative specifications for the transport index (for example trade volumes or pooled estimation with industry) and document the result, or obtain a dispensation.

deficiencies.rationale: The model is benchmarked only against its predecessor version 1.3; for a Tier 1 model MRM-STD-020 §9.1 requires a challenger model or an external or internal benchmark, and the comparison with the external rating agency study is qualitative only.

mitigation.text: Add a quantitative external benchmark (for example PIT PDs implied by the external default study per sector) or a challenger model to MDD section 7.2 before gate G1.

deficiencies.rationale: The MDD documents calibration of the PIT PDs to 2023–2025 default rates adjusted to current conditions, but Model Validation's replication per sector shows that the real estate and construction PIT PD underpredicts the 2025 default rate by 35% (1.9% against 2.9% for 2025 alone), because the real estate Z is dominated by the 2008–2013 cycle and the 2023–2025 calibration is applied at portfolio level only.

mitigation.text: Recalibrate the PIT PDs per sector group on 2023–2025 and keep overlay OVL-C-01 until the recalibration is validated.

deficiencies.rationale: MDD section 7.3 covers the key assumptions, but varies the asset correlations only by ±1 standard error; Model Validation's sensitivity with the correlations of the IRB supervisory formula range (0.12–0.24) changes the Stage 1 and 2 ECL by −9% to +22%, which shows that the correlation assumption is the dominant source of uncertainty and is not reflected in the documented range.

mitigation.text: Extend the sensitivity analysis to plausible alternative correlation estimates and document the choice of the maximum-likelihood estimates, including their effect on SICR transfers.
